title: Sowing sunflower shoots
subtitle: How to pre-soak and sow a sunflower shoot tray, from seed to the start of blackout
excerpt: Sunflower shoots need an 8 hour pre-soak before sowing. The large in-shell seed must be unhulled (not shelled kernels). After soaking, spread the seeds densely in a single layer on a 25 cm tray and blackout under a substantial weight to aid hull separation.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Soaking large, hard-coated seeds (peas, sunflowers, beans) in room-temperature water for 6 to 12 hours before sowing. The water penetrates the seed coat, triggers the germination signal, and dramatically reduces the time to the first visible shoot.

The period immediately after sowing when a second tray is stacked on top, blocking light from the sown tray. In darkness, germinating seeds direct energy into pushing the shoot upward rather than greening. The substantial weight used for sunflower seeds during this phase also helps the seed hulls separate from the emerging cotyledons.

content.text: Sowing sunflower shoots requires the same overnight pre-soak as pea shoots, plus one important seed-selection check: the seed must be in-shell (unhulled), the striped grey-and-white sunflower seed with the hull intact. Shelled sunflower kernels (the white seeds sold as bird food or snack food) will not germinate and should not be used.

One 25 cm × 25 cm growing tray. A second tray for the blackout cover. Seed compost. In-shell sunflower seed: 150 to 200 g per tray. A bowl for soaking. A substantial flat weight for the blackout phase: 1 to 2 kg is ideal (a bag of flour, a bag of rice, or a heavy flat object).

150 to 200 g of in-shell sunflower seed in a bowl of room-temperature water for 8 hours. The seeds absorb water noticeably; the hull softens slightly. Over-soaking beyond 12 hours can reduce germination rates; set a reminder if soaking overnight.
Step 1: drain and rinse. Drain the soak water (which contains surface sugars; rinsing prevents mould). The soaked seeds should be plump and slightly tacky.
Step 2: fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost, leaving 2 cm from the rim. Level the surface.

Step 3: spread the soaked seeds in a dense single layer. Sunflower seeds are large; aim for seeds touching but not stacked. Do not cover the seeds with compost; they germinate well when resting on the surface.
Step 4: press firmly. Press all seeds into contact with the medium beneath with a flat board or the base of the second tray.

: stack the second tray on top and place 1 to 2 kg of weight on it. The weight for sunflower is heavier than for other crops: the sunflower shoot pushes up with considerable force, and the resistance from the weight is what causes the hull to separate from the cotyledon as the shoot emerges. Leave for three days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common sowing-stage problems with sunflower shoots.

items.symptom: Seeds fail to germinate at all
items.cause: Shelled kernels (hulled groats) used instead of in-shell seed. Heat-treated seeds used.
items.fix: Check the seed: in-shell sunflower seed is the grey and white striped seed that looks like bird feeder sunflower seed. Kernels (fully white or cream) won't germinate. Buy from a microgreen seed supplier.

items.symptom: Mould on the soaked seeds within day 1 of the tray
items.cause: Soaking water not rinsed off, or seeds soaked too long.
items.fix: Rinse thoroughly after soaking. Reduce soak time to 8 hours on the next attempt. The soak water becomes progressively more sugar-rich; a thorough rinse removes most of the mould substrate.

items.symptom: Hulls all remain attached after the blackout phase
items.cause: Weight too light during blackout, or insufficient soak time.
items.fix: Increase the weight on the next batch to 1.5 to 2 kg. Ensure the soak time is a full 8 hours to soften the hull.
